title: 'The Punk Rockers': A Photo of Spiky Egret Chicks Wins Smithsonian's Top Prize
summary: They're fluffy, they're feisty, and they've got the attitude of a rock band. Three egret chicks, photographed mid-squabble at a New Jersey rookery, have won the grand prize in Smithsonian Magazine's 23rd annual Photo Contest. Jacqueline Burke, a 64-year-old veterinarian and photographer, titled her image "The Punk Rockers" because the chicks' spiked plumage gives them the unmistakable look of tiny mohawks. Burke captured the moment under a ramp at the Ocean City welcome center, where hundreds of birds were nesting. "They were squabbling nonstop," she said. "Their little necks and heads were writhing. One would peck. The other would peck back." The composition is striking: the chicks, each no larger than a golf ball when curled up, dominate the foreground, while their parent looms in the background—long, gnarly legs and imposing feet creating a dramatic scale jump. Smithsonian creative director Maria Keehan praised the framing, noting how the contrast between the delicate chicks and the adult's powerful feet makes the image remarkable. The contest drew more than 17,000 submissions from 108 countries. Other winning photographs include a barefoot devotee during a Hindu festival, a Navajo teenager's Kinaaldá ceremony with her horse, a chameleon glowing in a garden, and a drone shot of a circular R&D center in China. Burke, who traded bird-watching binoculars for a camera in 2014, says her love of animals drives her photography. "We need to save species like this and save moments like this," she said. Her winning image freezes a fleeting instant of wild, unpolished life—a reminder that nature's most captivating scenes are often the ones filled with noise, chaos, and a little bit of punk-rock spirit.
why_it_matters: This photo reminds young people that extraordinary moments exist in ordinary places—a parking lot rookery, not a remote wilderness. It encourages them to look closer at the natural world around them and consider how even 'common' species like egrets have faced extinction and need protection.

background_read: The Smithsonian Magazine Photo Contest is an annual competition that draws entries from around the world, often celebrating fleeting moments in nature and culture.
This year's grand prize went to a shot of great egret chicks—a species whose feathery plumes were once hunted to near extinction for women's hats in the 19th century.
Ocean City, New Jersey, where the photo was taken, is a barrier island known for its large shorebird colonies.
Another awarded image, a Kinaaldá ceremony (a traditional Navajo puberty rite for girls), highlights the contest's embrace of diverse cultural traditions.
Burke's win reflects a growing trend of amateur photographers—she only switched from binoculars to a camera in 2014—capturing remarkable wildlife scenes with professional-quality results.

perspectives.description: For Jacqueline Burke, winning validates her passion and proves that dedication to a craft can pay off later in life. Nature photographers and bird enthusiasts celebrate the image as a vibrant showcase of wildlife behavior and the importance of local habitats.

Some critics might argue that awarding a photo of common egrets overlooks more endangered or rare species. The contest could face pressure to prioritize conservation-focused images over purely aesthetic or humorous shots.

The photo's composition—juxtaposing fragile chicks with an imposing adult—plays on scale and tension, a classic technique that resonates with viewers. The contest's selection also reflects a broader trend in photography toward celebrating spontaneity and imperfection over studio perfection.

As attention grows, the winning image could spark increased funding or volunteer efforts for coastal bird conservation in New Jersey. It may also inspire more amateur photographers to document local wildlife, creating a grassroots visual record of biodiversity.
